title: Longmont Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Longmont wells have a 30 ft median depth, but fractured bedrock, yield, permits, and full installation costs still matter.
h1: Longmont, Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost
intro_html:
Buying land or a home near Longmont means looking past the well permit alone. Records within 5 miles show 1,626 permitted wells, with 850 recorded as constructed. The local data points to shallow wells overall, but fractured mountain bedrock can make individual drilling results unpredictable.

This page covers well depth, production, water levels, permit history, drilling costs, and the environmental and septic questions to resolve before closing or starting construction. Nearby records from Niwot, Mead, Frederick, Firestone, Leyner, and Gunbarrel can also provide useful comparison points, but a neighboring well is not a guarantee for your lot.

sections.heading: Longmont well depth depends on the ground below the lot
sections.html:
The median reported well depth near Longmont is 30 feet. The middle half runs from 16 to 50 feet, so a bid based on the typical local depth may be reasonable for some sites. Still, the range is wide: the 90th-percentile depth is 158 feet, and the deepest record reaches 600 feet.

Most recorded wells are under 100 feet, while 8% fall between 100 and 300 feet and 5% extend from 300 to 600 feet. The aquifer designation matters. Records name an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer for 1,328 wells, compared with 112 alluvial wells and 16 Quaternary Alluvium wells. Granite and gneiss can fracture irregularly, so nearby depth is a guide, not a promise.

sections.heading: What Longmont wells produce for a household
sections.html:
Among the 93 records that report pump yield, the median is 12.0 gallons per minute. The middle half is 10.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. Forty-seven percent report 5 to 15 gallons per minute, and 46% report more than 15 gallons per minute. No reported well falls under 1 gallon per minute.

That is a strong result in the available records, but the sample is much smaller than the total permit count. Yield also depends on the test, pump setup, storage, and the well’s intended use. Ask for the well-completion report and pump test, not just a seller’s statement that the well “has water.” A domestic or household-use well still needs a suitable pump, pressure system, and storage arrangement.

sections.heading: Longmont water levels look shallow, but the trend is limited
sections.html:
Only 53 records report a static water level, so the water-level sample is limited. In those records, the median depth to water is 10 feet, with the middle half from 8 to 11 feet. That suggests many tested wells encountered relatively shallow standing water.

The available facts do not provide a water-level series by decade, so they cannot establish that the local water table is dropping or rising. Static level is also not the same as pumping level. A buyer should ask when the measurement was taken, whether the well had rested before testing, and how much the level changed while pumping. Casing and grout details matter as well, especially where shallow groundwater may be exposed to surface sources.

sections.heading: Longmont permit history shows current drilling activity
sections.html:
Colorado DWR permit records are the starting point for checking a well’s legal status, permitted use, construction report, and recorded depth. The Longmont search area includes permits issued as recently as 2025. Forty-six permits were issued in the 2020s, while the full record contains 1,626 permits.

The records identify Authorized (Pe, Pg) as the most active driller, with 534 entries. Marshall Drilling, listed as Marshall, James C, appears on 88, and Harry Young Drilling, listed as Young, Harry J, appears on 17. These names describe the permit history; they are not a substitute for inspecting the well or confirming who is available for new work. Check the permit number, use type, construction report, and any change-of-use requirements before relying on the water right.

sections.heading: A Longmont well can cost more than the hole itself
sections.html:
Local drilling is modeled as fractured mountain bedrock, including granite and gneiss, at about $65 to $100 per foot. At the 30-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $2,000 to $3,000. That is only the drilling portion, not the complete water system.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $8,000 to $15,000 at the median depth. A deeper hole, difficult access, casing or grout requirements, and site-specific electrical or trench work can change the bid. Ask the driller to separate footage, casing, grout, development, pump equipment, pressure system, trenching, electrical, testing, and permit-related work so competing bids can be compared fairly.

sections.heading: Environmental, septic, and dry-hole checks near Longmont
sections.html:
Mapped environmental records within about 10 miles include 568 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 41 historic mine features, and 8 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. A mapped site does not automatically mean a particular parcel’s well is contaminated, but it is a reason to review the site history and test existing water. Ask for current laboratory results covering the concerns identified for the property.

Low yield is not the only risk. A fractured-bedrock well can miss a productive fracture or require more depth than nearby records suggest. Septic setbacks, soil conditions, well location, access for a rig, and space for a replacement system should be checked before building. If the basin is over-appropriated, an augmentation plan or other water-right requirements may affect new household use.

sections.heading: What to verify before buying a Longmont-area lot
sections.html:
Start with the DWR file for the exact parcel or home. Confirm the permit, permitted use, construction report, total depth, pump yield, static level, casing and grout, and the current pump and pressure equipment. The use mix in the records includes 33% domestic or household, 4% stock, 4% irrigation, and 43% monitoring, so the nearest permit may not be comparable to a home well.

For a vacant lot, obtain a written drilling and complete-system estimate and confirm where a rig, driveway, septic system, and electrical service can fit. For an existing home, make the sale contingent on water-quality and flow testing, inspection of the wellhead and pressure system, and review of repair history. Compare several nearby wells, including records around Niwot, Gunbarrel, and Mead, while treating every result as site-specific.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Longmont, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within 5 miles of Longmont is 30 feet, and the middle half runs from 16 to 50 feet. Eighty-seven percent are under 100 feet. Depth can vary sharply in fractured granite and gneiss, however; the 90th-percentile depth is 158 feet and the deepest record is 600 feet.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Longmont?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $65 to $100 per foot. At the 30-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at about $2,000 to $3,000. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $8,000 to $15,000. Difficult access, deeper drilling, and site conditions can raise the final bid.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Longmont?
faq.a: Only 93 records report a pump yield, but those show a 12.0-gallon-per-minute median and a 10.0-to-15.0 middle half. Forty-seven percent report 5 to 15 gallons per minute, while 46% report more than 15. No reported well is under 1 gallon per minute. A pump test is still important for a specific property.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Longmont?
faq.a: The records alone cannot establish that a home’s water is safe. Within about 10 miles, mapped records include 568 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 41 historic mine features, and 8 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Have the property’s water tested by a laboratory, review its location and history, and do not rely only on a nearby well’s result.

faq.q: Can I build a home on a well near Longmont?
faq.a: Possibly, but confirm the permit and permitted use, well yield, septic feasibility, access, and water-right requirements first. Domestic or household permits make up 33% of the use mix in these records, while many others are monitoring wells. In an over-appropriated basin, an augmentation plan may be required. A Colorado DWR file and site-specific septic review are essential.
